claim: CMT2A is an untreatable childhood peripheral neuropathy caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin (MFN) 2.
source: Charcot–Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) is an untreatable childhood peripheral neuropathy caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin (MFN) 2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about CMT2A and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological activation of endogenous normal mitofusins overcame dominant inhibitory effects of CMT2A mutants in reprogrammed human patient motor neurons.
source: Here, pharmacological activation of endogenous normal mitofusins overcame dominant inhibitory effects of CMT2A mutants in reprogrammed human patient motor neurons, reversing hallmark mitochondrial stasis and fragmentation independent of causal MFN2 mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c demonstrating improvements in mitochondrial aspect ratio, depolarization, and motility across four different CMT2A patient mutations.

claim: Mitofusin activation reversed mitochondrial stasis and fragmentation independent of causal MFN2 mutation.
source: Here, pharmacological activation of endogenous normal mitofusins overcame dominant inhibitory effects of CMT2A mutants in reprogrammed human patient motor neurons, reversing hallmark mitochondrial stasis and fragmentation independent of causal MFN2 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by data from four different CMT2A patient lines with different MFN2 mutations (T105M, R274W, H361Y, R364W) all showing similar improvements with mitofusin activator treatment (Figure 1c).

claim: Intermittent mitofusin activation with MiM111 normalized CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction in mice expressing human MFN2 T105M.
source: In mice expressing human MFN2 T105M, intermittent mitofusin activation with a small molecule, MiM111, normalized CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction, reversed pre-treatment axon and skeletal myocyte atrophy, and enhanced axon regrowth by increasing mitochondrial transport within peripheral axons and promoting in vivo mitochondrial localization to neuromuscular junctional synapses.
evidence: This is supported by RotaRod and CMAP data in Figure 3c and d showing functional improvement in MFN2 T105M mice treated with MiM111.

claim: MiM111 treatment reversed pre-treatment axon and skeletal myocyte atrophy in MFN2 T105M mice.
source: In mice expressing human MFN2 T105M, intermittent mitofusin activation with a small molecule, MiM111, normalized CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction, reversed pre-treatment axon and skeletal myocyte atrophy, and enhanced axon regrowth by increasing mitochondrial transport within peripheral axons and promoting in vivo mitochondrial localization to neuromuscular junctional synapses.
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 4b and c showing increased axon diameter and myocyte cross-sectional area after MiM111 treatment.

claim: MiM111 enhanced axon regrowth by increasing mitochondrial transport within peripheral axons.
source: In mice expressing human MFN2 T105M, intermittent mitofusin activation with a small molecule, MiM111, normalized CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction, reversed pre-treatment axon and skeletal myocyte atrophy, and enhanced axon regrowth by increasing mitochondrial transport within peripheral axons and promoting in vivo mitochondrial localization to neuromuscular junctional synapses.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing increased mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons after MiM111 treatment.

claim: MiM111 promoted in vivo mitochondrial localization to neuromuscular junctional synapses.
source: In mice expressing human MFN2 T105M, intermittent mitofusin activation with a small molecule, MiM111, normalized CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction, reversed pre-treatment axon and skeletal myocyte atrophy, and enhanced axon regrowth by increasing mitochondrial transport within peripheral axons and promoting in vivo mitochondrial localization to neuromuscular junctional synapses.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 4d showing increased mitochondrial occupancy in neuromuscular synaptic junctions after MiM111 treatment.

claim: MiM111-treated MFN2 T105M mouse neurons exhibited accelerated primary outgrowth.
source: MiM111-treated MFN2 T105M mouse neurons exhibited accelerated primary outgrowth and greater post-axotomy regrowth, linked to enhanced mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing increased neuronal process length and branching in CMT2A DRG neurons treated with MiM111.

claim: MiM111-treated MFN2 T105M mouse neurons exhibited greater post-axotomy regrowth.
source: MiM111-treated MFN2 T105M mouse neurons exhibited accelerated primary outgrowth and greater post-axotomy regrowth, linked to enhanced mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing increased axon length after axotomy in MiM111-treated CMT2A cortical neurons.

claim: MiM111 is the first pre-clinical candidate for CMT2A.
source: MiM111 is the first pre-clinical candidate for CMT2A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comprehensive preclinical data presented in the manuscript showing efficacy in multiple models.

claim: Type 2A CMT (CMT2A) is caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin 2 (MFN2).
source: Type 2A CMT (CMT2A) is caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin 2 (MFN2) (Züchner et al., 2004), and is distinguished from other CMT subtypes by onset of neuromuscular signs in early childhood and progressive loss of neuromuscular coordination and strength in arms throughout the first two decades of life, thought to be the consequence of dying-back of long peripheral nerves (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Züchner et al., 2004 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: CMT2A is distinguished from other CMT subtypes by onset of neuromuscular signs in early childhood.
source: Type 2A CMT (CMT2A) is caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin 2 (MFN2) (Züchner et al., 2004), and is distinguished from other CMT subtypes by onset of neuromuscular signs in early childhood and progressive loss of neuromuscular coordination and strength in arms throughout the first two decades of life, thought to be the consequence of dying-back of long peripheral nerves (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017) describing clinical characteristics of CMT2A.

claim: CMT2A involves progressive loss of neuromuscular coordination and strength in arms throughout the first two decades of life.
source: Type 2A CMT (CMT2A) is caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin 2 (MFN2) (Züchner et al., 2004), and is distinguished from other CMT subtypes by onset of neuromuscular signs in early childhood and progressive loss of neuromuscular coordination and strength in arms throughout the first two decades of life, thought to be the consequence of dying-back of long peripheral nerves (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the clinical progression of CMT2A.

claim: CMT2A pathology is thought to be the consequence of dying-back of long peripheral nerves.
source: Type 2A CMT (CMT2A) is caused by mutations of the mitochondrial fusion protein, mitofusin 2 (MFN2) (Züchner et al., 2004), and is distinguished from other CMT subtypes by onset of neuromuscular signs in early childhood and progressive loss of neuromuscular coordination and strength in arms throughout the first two decades of life, thought to be the consequence of dying-back of long peripheral nerves (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations and represents current understanding in the field.

claim: There are currently no disease-modifying treatments for CMT2A.
source: Because there are currently no disease-modifying treatments, CMT2A is managed with braces, wheelchairs, and social support.
evidence: This represents current clinical knowledge about CMT2A treatment options.

claim: CMT2A is managed with braces, wheelchairs, and social support.
source: Because there are currently no disease-modifying treatments, CMT2A is managed with braces, wheelchairs, and social support.
evidence: This represents current clinical practice for managing CMT2A symptoms.

claim: Over 100 different dominant missense MFN2 mutations are implicated in CMT2A.
source: Over 100 different dominant missense MFN2 mutations are implicated in CMT2A (Beręsewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beręsewicz et al., 2018.

claim: MFN2 and related MFN1 are nuclear-encoded dynamin-family GTPases located at the mitochondrial outer membrane-cytosol interface.
source: MFN2 and related MFN1 are nuclear-encoded dynamin-family GTPases located at the mitochondrial outer membrane-cytosol interface where they promote mitochondrial fusion essential to mitochondrial respiratory function and repair (Chan, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MFN proteins supported by citation to Chan, 2012.

claim: MFN1 and MFN2 promote mitochondrial fusion essential to mitochondrial respiratory function and repair.
source: MFN2 and related MFN1 are nuclear-encoded dynamin-family GTPases located at the mitochondrial outer membrane-cytosol interface where they promote mitochondrial fusion essential to mitochondrial respiratory function and repair (Chan, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MFN function supported by citation to Chan, 2012.

claim: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of mitochondrial fusion is proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
source: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of mitochondrial fusion (Chen and Chan, 2006; Pareyson et al., 2015), mitophagy (Rizzo et al., 2016; Filadi et al., 2018), and/or neuronal mitochondrial transport (Pareyson et al., 2015; Baloh et al., 2007; Crunkhorn, 2018) are proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of mitophagy is proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
source: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of mitochondrial fusion (Chen and Chan, 2006; Pareyson et al., 2015), mitophagy (Rizzo et al., 2016; Filadi et al., 2018), and/or neuronal mitochondrial transport (Pareyson et al., 2015; Baloh et al., 2007; Crunkhorn, 2018) are proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to Rizzo et al., 2016 and Filadi et al., 2018.

claim: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of neuronal mitochondrial transport is proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
source: Dominant inhibition by MFN2 mutants of mitochondrial fusion (Chen and Chan, 2006; Pareyson et al., 2015), mitophagy (Rizzo et al., 2016; Filadi et al., 2018), and/or neuronal mitochondrial transport (Pareyson et al., 2015; Baloh et al., 2007; Crunkhorn, 2018) are proposed to evoke neuronal degeneration in CMT2A.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: CMT2A is an autosomal dominant genetic condition.
source: Because CMT2A is an autosomal dominant genetic condition, gene editing could potentially correct causal MFN2 mutant alleles, but the large number of different causal CMT2A MFN2 mutations complicates an editing approach.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the inheritance pattern of CMT2A.

claim: The large number of different causal CMT2A MFN2 mutations complicates a gene editing approach.
source: Because CMT2A is an autosomal dominant genetic condition, gene editing could potentially correct causal MFN2 mutant alleles, but the large number of different causal CMT2A MFN2 mutations complicates an editing approach.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the diversity of mutations and the specificity required for gene editing.

claim: Forced expression of normal mitofusins can oppose mutant MFN2 dysfunction in transgenic mice.
source: Alternately, forced expression of normal mitofusins could oppose mutant MFN2 dysfunction, as demonstrated in a recent study in transgenic mice (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: MFN gene therapy would be difficult to discontinue or reverse if adverse effects of MFN overactivity are encountered.
source: However, MFN gene therapy would be difficult to discontinue or reverse if postulated adverse effects of MFN overactivity are encountered (El Fissi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a logical inference about gene therapy limitations, supported by citation to El Fissi et al., 2018 regarding potential adverse effects.

claim: Pharmacological mitofusin activators improved mitochondrial morphology, fitness, and motility in human and mouse CMT2A neurons in vitro.
source: Pharmacological mitofusin activators improved mitochondrial morphology, fitness, and motility in human and mouse CMT2A neurons in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1c, 2f, and 5 showing improvements in these parameters.

claim: Daily administration of a short acting mitofusin activator to mice with late stage CMT2A reversed neuromuscular dysfunction.
source: Daily administration of a short acting mitofusin activator to mice with late stage CMT2A reversed neuromuscular dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3c and d showing improvement in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude.

claim: Neuronal repair and regeneration in CMT2A were linked to enhanced mitochondrial transport to axonal termini.
source: Mechanistically, neuronal repair and regeneration were linked to enhanced mitochondrial transport to, and mitochondrial occupation within, axonal termini.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased mitochondrial motility (Figures 3a, 5) and increased mitochondrial occupancy at neuromuscular junctions (Figure 4d).

claim: Neuronal repair and regeneration in CMT2A were linked to mitochondrial occupation within axonal termini.
source: Mechanistically, neuronal repair and regeneration were linked to enhanced mitochondrial transport to, and mitochondrial occupation within, axonal termini.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing increased mitochondrial occupancy in neuromuscular synaptic junctions after MiM111 treatment.

claim: Reversal of pre-existing CMT2A neuromuscular degeneration in vivo has not previously been achieved by any means.
source: Reversal of pre-existing CMT2A neuromuscular degeneration in vivo has not previously been achieved by any means, and provides a powerful rationale for advancing mitofusin activators to first in human trials.
evidence: This represents a claim about the novelty of the findings based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Common MFN2 GTPase and coiled-coiled domain mutations induce more severe and earlier onset CMT2A disease.
source: Common MFN2 GTPase and coiled-coiled domain mutations induce more severe and earlier onset disease, whereas rare carboxy terminal domain mutations confer later onset and milder disease (Feely et al., 2011; Stuppia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feely et al., 2011 and Stuppia et al., 2015.

claim: Rare MFN2 carboxy terminal domain mutations confer later onset and milder CMT2A disease.
source: Common MFN2 GTPase and coiled-coiled domain mutations induce more severe and earlier onset disease, whereas rare carboxy terminal domain mutations confer later onset and milder disease (Feely et al., 2011; Stuppia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feely et al., 2011 and Stuppia et al., 2015.

claim: All four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited fragmented mitochondria compared to normal neurons.
source: Compared to neurons reprogrammed from individuals with no evident disease at the time of sampling and who had none of the tested MFN2 mutations by Sanger sequencing ('normal'), all four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited fragmented mitochondria (decreased mitochondrial aspect ratio; length/width) that is a consequence of impaired fusion in this context Franco et al., 2016; accompanying mitochondrial depolarization reflected characteristic functional impairment (Figure 1c; Crowley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing decreased mitochondrial aspect ratio in all four CMT2A patient lines.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial aspect ratio is a consequence of impaired fusion in CMT2A.
source: Compared to neurons reprogrammed from individuals with no evident disease at the time of sampling and who had none of the tested MFN2 mutations by Sanger sequencing ('normal'), all four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited fragmented mitochondria (decreased mitochondrial aspect ratio; length/width) that is a consequence of impaired fusion in this context Franco et al., 2016; accompanying mitochondrial depolarization reflected characteristic functional impairment (Figure 1c; Crowley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2016 and represents established understanding of the relationship between fusion and mitochondrial morphology.

claim: All four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Compared to neurons reprogrammed from individuals with no evident disease at the time of sampling and who had none of the tested MFN2 mutations by Sanger sequencing ('normal'), all four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited fragmented mitochondria (decreased mitochondrial aspect ratio; length/width) that is a consequence of impaired fusion in this context Franco et al., 2016; accompanying mitochondrial depolarization reflected characteristic functional impairment (Figure 1c; Crowley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing increased % depolarized mitochondria in all four CMT2A patient lines.

claim: All four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited abnormal mitochondrial transport through axons.
source: Moreover, all four CMT2A motor neuron lines exhibited abnormal mitochondrial transport through axons, with diminished proportion and velocity of motile mitochondria (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing decreased motile mitochondria percentage and velocity in all four CMT2A patient lines.

claim: Mitochondrial fragmentation, respiratory dysfunction, and dysmotility observed in reprogrammed neurons are prototypical features of CMT2A.
source: Mitochondrial fragmentation, respiratory dysfunction, and dysmotility observed in reprogrammed neurons are prototypical features of CMT2A (Baloh et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2019; Verhoeven et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing these features in CMT2A.

claim: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) improved mitochondrial aspect ratio in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) also improved mitochondrial aspect ratio, depolarization, and motility in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing increased aspect ratio after Chimera C treatment in all four patient lines.

claim: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) improved mitochondrial depolarization in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) also improved mitochondrial aspect ratio, depolarization, and motility in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing decreased % depolarized mitochondria after Chimera C treatment in all four patient lines.

claim: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) improved mitochondrial motility in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) also improved mitochondrial aspect ratio, depolarization, and motility in all four CMT2A patient motor neuron lines (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1c showing increased motile mitochondria percentage and velocity after Chimera C treatment in all four patient lines.

claim: No mouse models of CMT2A recapitulate all key clinical features in the absence of confounding developmental phenotypes.
source: No mouse models of CMT2A recapitulate all of these key clinical features in the absence of confounding developmental phenotypes (Zhou et al., 2019; Detmer et al., 2008; Cartoni et al., 2010; Bannerman et al., 2016; Dorn, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple mouse model studies.

claim: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice was normal at 10 weeks of age.
source: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice was normal at 10 weeks of age, progressively declined thereafter, and stabilized beyond 30 weeks (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2c showing no difference between CMT2A and WT mice at 10 weeks.

claim: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice progressively declined after 10 weeks of age.
source: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice was normal at 10 weeks of age, progressively declined thereafter, and stabilized beyond 30 weeks (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2c showing progressive decline in RotaRod performance from 10 to 30 weeks.

claim: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice stabilized beyond 30 weeks of age.
source: RotaRod latency of CMT2A mice was normal at 10 weeks of age, progressively declined thereafter, and stabilized beyond 30 weeks (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2c showing stable RotaRod performance from 30 to 50 weeks.

claim: Axonal mitochondria of MFN2 T105M mice were fragmented with disorganized cristae.
source: As in clinical CMT2A, axonal mitochondria of MFN2 T105M mice were fragmented with disorganized cristae (Sole et al., 2009; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 2d and citation to Sole et al., 2009.

claim: Sciatic nerve-tibialis muscle CMAP amplitudes of 50-week-old MFN2 T105M mice were diminished with no change in signal latency.
source: Recapitulating this clinical finding, sciatic nerve-tibialis muscle CMAP amplitudes of 50-week-old MFN2 T105M mice were diminished with no change in signal latency, which reflects conduction velocity (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by neuroelectrophysiology data in Figure 2e showing decreased CMAP amplitude but normal latency.

claim: Neuroelectrophysiological testing of CMT2A patients characteristically reveals reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAP) with normal nerve conduction velocities.
source: Neuroelectrophysiological testing of CMT2A patients characteristically reveals reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAP) with normal nerve conduction velocities (Berciano et al., 2017; Harding and Thomas, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berciano et al., 2017 and Harding and Thomas, 1980.

claim: Mitofusin activation improved mitochondrial aspect ratio in CMT2A mouse DRG neurons.
source: As in reprogrammed human CMT2A motor neurons, mitofusin activation improved these abnormalities (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, compare to Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2f showing increased aspect ratio after Chimera C treatment in CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Mitofusin activation improved mitochondrial transport in CMT2A mouse DRG neurons.
source: As in reprogrammed human CMT2A motor neurons, mitofusin activation improved these abnormalities (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, compare to Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2f showing increased motile mitochondria percentage and velocity after Chimera C treatment in CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Mitofusin activation improved mitochondrial polarization status in CMT2A mouse DRG neurons.
source: As in reprogrammed human CMT2A motor neurons, mitofusin activation improved these abnormalities (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, compare to Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing increased TMRE fluorescence (indicating improved polarization) after Chimera C treatment in CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Chimera C is rapidly degraded by the liver and undergoes first-pass metabolism.
source: However, Chimera C is rapidly degraded by the liver and undergoes first-pass metabolism, making it impractical for in vivo studies (Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2020.

claim: MiM111 is a structurally distinct compound having a mitofusin activation profile similar to Chimera C.
source: We therefore evaluated in vivo efficacy of mitofusin activation in CMT2A using MiM111, a structurally distinct compound having a mitofusin activation profile similar to Chimera C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but which is metabolically stable with good nervous system bioavailability (Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing similar effects of MiM111 and Chimera C on mitochondrial parameters, and citation to Dang et al., 2020.

claim: MiM111 is metabolically stable with good nervous system bioavailability.
source: We therefore evaluated in vivo efficacy of mitofusin activation in CMT2A using MiM111, a structurally distinct compound having a mitofusin activation profile similar to Chimera C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but which is metabolically stable with good nervous system bioavailability (Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2020.

claim: Daily intramuscular dosing of MiM111 would reverse mitochondrial dysmotility in CMT2A mice for approximately 12 hr out of every 24 hr.
source: Based on a minimum effective MiM111 plasma concentration of 30 ng/ml (Dang et al., 2020) and a plasma t1/2 of 2.3 hr with Cmax of 24,000 ng/ml after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we estimated that daily IM dosing would reverse mitochondrial dysmotility in CMT2A mice for ~12 hr out of every 24 hr.
evidence: This is based on pharmacokinetic calculations using data from Dang et al., 2020 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice was normalized 4 hr after a single intramuscular injection of MiM111 (30 mg/kg).
source: Indeed, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 show that mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice was normalized 4 hr after a single intramuscular injection of MiM111 (30 mg/kg), declined by approximately half after 12 hr, and returned to CMT2A baseline after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c showing increased mitochondrial motility 4 hr after MiM111 injection.

claim: Mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice declined by approximately half 12 hr after MiM111 injection.
source: Indeed, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 show that mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice was normalized 4 hr after a single intramuscular injection of MiM111 (30 mg/kg), declined by approximately half after 12 hr, and returned to CMT2A baseline after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c showing partial decline in mitochondrial motility 12 hr after MiM111 injection.

claim: Mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice returned to CMT2A baseline 24 hr after MiM111 injection.
source: Indeed, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 show that mitochondrial motility in sciatic nerve axons of MFN2 T105M mice was normalized 4 hr after a single intramuscular injection of MiM111 (30 mg/kg), declined by approximately half after 12 hr, and returned to CMT2A baseline after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c showing return to baseline mitochondrial motility 24 hr after MiM111 injection.

claim: The characteristic decreases in RotaRod latency in MFN2 T105M mice were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment.
source: The characteristic decreases in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude in MFN2 T105M mice (see Figure 2c and e) were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment and remained near normal after 8 weeks (Figure 3c and d); MiM111 had no effect on control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3c showing increased RotaRod latency in MiM111-treated CMT2A mice at 4 weeks.

claim: The characteristic decreases in CMAP amplitude in MFN2 T105M mice were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment.
source: The characteristic decreases in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude in MFN2 T105M mice (see Figure 2c and e) were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment and remained near normal after 8 weeks (Figure 3c and d); MiM111 had no effect on control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3d showing increased CMAP amplitude in MiM111-treated CMT2A mice at 4 weeks.

claim: RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude remained near normal 8 weeks after MiM111 treatment in MFN2 T105M mice.
source: The characteristic decreases in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude in MFN2 T105M mice (see Figure 2c and e) were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment and remained near normal after 8 weeks (Figure 3c and d); MiM111 had no effect on control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3c and d showing sustained improvement in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude at 8 weeks.

claim: MiM111 had no effect on control mice.
source: The characteristic decreases in RotaRod latency and CMAP amplitude in MFN2 T105M mice (see Figure 2c and e) were reversed 4 weeks after MiM111 treatment and remained near normal after 8 weeks (Figure 3c and d); MiM111 had no effect on control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing no change in RotaRod latency or CMAP amplitude in wild-type mice treated with MiM111.

claim: MiM111 treatment reduced axon damage in sciatic nerves of MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice.
source: Compared to sciatic nerves of vehicle-treated MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice, MiM111 treatment reduced axon damage (Figure 4a), increased axon diameter (Figure 4b), and increased staining for superior cervical ganglion 10 (SCG10; a marker of neuron regeneration) (Shin et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing decreased percentage of damaged axons after MiM111 treatment.

claim: MiM111 treatment increased axon diameter in sciatic nerves of MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice.
source: Compared to sciatic nerves of vehicle-treated MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice, MiM111 treatment reduced axon damage (Figure 4a), increased axon diameter (Figure 4b), and increased staining for superior cervical ganglion 10 (SCG10; a marker of neuron regeneration) (Shin et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4b showing increased axon area after MiM111 treatment.

claim: MiM111 treatment increased staining for SCG10 in sciatic nerves of MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice.
source: Compared to sciatic nerves of vehicle-treated MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice, MiM111 treatment reduced axon damage (Figure 4a), increased axon diameter (Figure 4b), and increased staining for superior cervical ganglion 10 (SCG10; a marker of neuron regeneration) (Shin et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing increased percentage of SCG10-positive axons after MiM111 treatment.

claim: SCG10 is a marker of neuron regeneration.
source: Compared to sciatic nerves of vehicle-treated MFN2 T105M CMT2A mice, MiM111 treatment reduced axon damage (Figure 4a), increased axon diameter (Figure 4b), and increased staining for superior cervical ganglion 10 (SCG10; a marker of neuron regeneration) (Shin et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shin et al., 2014.

claim: Mitofusin activation reversed CMT2A-induced neuronal degeneration.
source: These findings suggest that mitofusin activation reversed CMT2A-induced neuronal degeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing reduced axon damage, increased axon diameter, and increased regeneration markers after MiM111 treatment.

claim: Skeletal myocytes of CMT2A mouse tibialis muscle were abnormally small.
source: Skeletal myocytes of CMT2A mouse tibialis muscle innervated by the sciatic nerve were abnormally small (Figure 4c), reflecting neurogenic muscle atrophy (because the MFN2 T105M transgene is directed by neuron-specific HB9-Cre).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4c showing decreased myocyte cross-sectional area in CMT2A mice.

claim: Small myocyte size in CMT2A mice reflects neurogenic muscle atrophy.
source: Skeletal myocytes of CMT2A mouse tibialis muscle innervated by the sciatic nerve were abnormally small (Figure 4c), reflecting neurogenic muscle atrophy (because the MFN2 T105M transgene is directed by neuron-specific HB9-Cre).
evidence: This is an inference based on the neuron-specific expression of the MFN2 T105M transgene.

claim: Skeletal myocyte mitochondria of CMT2A mice appeared structurally normal.
source: In agreement with muscle atrophy being a secondary effect, skeletal myocyte mitochondria of CMT2A mice appeared structurally normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) compare to sciatic nerve axon mitochondria in Figures 2d and 4b.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b showing normal mitochondrial area in tibialis muscle.

claim: Normalization of tibialis myocyte diameter after mitofusin activation indicates restoration of neuromuscular integrity.
source: Therefore, normalization of tibialis myocyte diameter after mitofusin activation (Figure 4c) indicates restoration of neuromuscular integrity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased myocyte cross-sectional area after MiM111 treatment (Figure 4c).

claim: CMT2A mice had approximately 50% fewer neuromuscular synaptic junctions per myocyte compared to normal mice.
source: Compared to normal mice, CMT2A mice had ~50% fewer synaptic junctions/myocyte, which was reversed after mitofusin activator treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing decreased synapses per myocyte in vehicle-treated CMT2A mice.

claim: Reduced neuromuscular junction density in CMT2A mice was reversed after mitofusin activator treatment.
source: Compared to normal mice, CMT2A mice had ~50% fewer synaptic junctions/myocyte, which was reversed after mitofusin activator treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing increased synapses per myocyte in MiM111-treated CMT2A mice.

claim: Mitochondrial occupancy of vehicle-treated CMT2A neuromuscular synaptic junctions was reduced by approximately half compared to normal mice.
source: Strikingly, mitochondrial occupancy of vehicle-treated CMT2A neuromuscular synaptic junctions was also reduced by ~half compared to normal mice, and was normalized by MiM111 treatment (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing decreased Cox IV/AchR pixel intensity in vehicle-treated CMT2A mice.

claim: Mitochondrial occupancy of CMT2A neuromuscular synaptic junctions was normalized by MiM111 treatment.
source: Strikingly, mitochondrial occupancy of vehicle-treated CMT2A neuromuscular synaptic junctions was also reduced by ~half compared to normal mice, and was normalized by MiM111 treatment (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing increased Cox IV/AchR pixel intensity in MiM111-treated CMT2A mice.

claim: Mitochondrial transport can play a central role in neuron repair and regeneration.
source: Because mitochondrial transport can play a central role in neuron repair and regeneration (Sheng, 2017), the observation that MiM111 promoted mitochondrial localization within terminal neuromuscular synaptic junctions provided a plausible mechanistic link between mitofusin activation, mitochondrial motility, neuronal regrowth, and reversal of neuromuscular dysfunction in this preclinical CMT2A model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheng, 2017.

claim: MiM111 promotion of mitochondrial localization within terminal neuromuscular synaptic junctions provides a plausible mechanistic link between mitofusin activation, mitochondrial motility, neuronal regrowth, and reversal of neuromuscular dysfunction.
source: Because mitochondrial transport can play a central role in neuron repair and regeneration (Sheng, 2017), the observation that MiM111 promoted mitochondrial localization within terminal neuromuscular synaptic junctions provided a plausible mechanistic link between mitofusin activation, mitochondrial motility, neuronal regrowth, and reversal of neuromuscular dysfunction in this preclinical CMT2A model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased mitochondrial occupancy at synapses (Figure 4d) and the established role of mitochondrial transport in neuronal function.

claim: Sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited enhanced mitochondrial fusion.
source: Indeed, sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited not only enhanced mitochondrial fusion (increased aspect ratio) and transport (greater mitochondrial motility and velocity), but axon outgrowth (length and branching) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5c showing increased mitochondrial aspect ratio in MiM111-treated CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited enhanced mitochondrial transport.
source: Indeed, sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited not only enhanced mitochondrial fusion (increased aspect ratio) and transport (greater mitochondrial motility and velocity), but axon outgrowth (length and branching) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5d and e showing increased mitochondrial motility and velocity in MiM111-treated CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited enhanced axon outgrowth.
source: Indeed, sensory DRG neurons isolated from CMT2A mice and cultured in the presence of MiM111 (100 nM, 48 hr) exhibited not only enhanced mitochondrial fusion (increased aspect ratio) and transport (greater mitochondrial motility and velocity), but axon outgrowth (length and branching) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5e showing increased neuronal process length and branching in MiM111-treated CMT2A DRG neurons.

claim: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) produced similar effects to MiM111 in CMT2A DRG neurons.
source: Similar effects were seen in CMT2A DRGs treated with Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing similar improvements in mitochondrial parameters and axon outgrowth with Chimera C treatment.

claim: Both MiM111 and Chimera C provoked mitochondrial redistribution to axonal termini of cultured CMT2A DRGs.
source: Both MiM111 and Chimera C provoked mitochondrial redistribution to axonal termini of cultured CMT2A DRGs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) recapitulating mitochondrial occupation of neuromuscular synapses after MiM111 treatment of CMT2A mice in vivo (see Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c showing increased proportion of neuronal process termini containing mitochondria after treatment.

claim: The increase in mitochondrial motility after mitofusin activation was rapid, being half-maximal after 2 hr.
source: Comparing the mitochondrial motility, aspect ratio, and neuron growth responses at different times after mitofusin activation revealed significantly increased mitochondrial trafficking within 2 hr, whereas enhanced axon outgrowth was significant after 24 and 28 hr, and mitochondrial aspect ratio (i.e. fusion) was significant only after 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing significant increase in mitochondrial motility at 2 hr.

claim: Enhanced axon outgrowth after mitofusin activation was significant after 24 hr.
source: Comparing the mitochondrial motility, aspect ratio, and neuron growth responses at different times after mitofusin activation revealed significantly increased mitochondrial trafficking within 2 hr, whereas enhanced axon outgrowth was significant after 24 and 28 hr, and mitochondrial aspect ratio (i.e. fusion) was significant only after 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing significant increase in neuron outgrowth at 24 hr.

claim: Increased mitochondrial aspect ratio after mitofusin activation was significant only after 48 hr.
source: Comparing the mitochondrial motility, aspect ratio, and neuron growth responses at different times after mitofusin activation revealed significantly increased mitochondrial trafficking within 2 hr, whereas enhanced axon outgrowth was significant after 24 and 28 hr, and mitochondrial aspect ratio (i.e. fusion) was significant only after 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing significant increase in aspect ratio only at 48 hr.

claim: The temporal sequence of mitochondrial motility increase preceding axon outgrowth lends credence to the idea that accelerated neuron growth is a consequence of enhanced mitochondrial function and redistribution.
source: Given the established role for mitochondrial transport in neuronal repair (Sheng, 2017), this temporal sequence lends credence to the idea that accelerated neuron growth is a consequence of enhanced mitochondrial function and redistribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation to Sheng, 2017.

claim: Mitochondrial motility was reduced by axotomy in cortical neurons.
source: By contrast, and consistent with a previous study in normal neurons (Zhou et al., 2016), mitochondrial motility was reduced by axotomy (Figure 6d middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing decreased mitochondrial motility after axotomy, and citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Mitofusin activation with MiM111 after axotomy restored mitochondrial motility to pre-axotomy levels.
source: Mitofusin activation with MiM111 after axotomy restored mitochondrial motility and neuronal outgrowth to pre-axotomy levels.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing increased mitochondrial motility in MiM111-treated neurons after axotomy.

claim: Mitofusin activation with MiM111 after axotomy restored neuronal outgrowth to pre-axotomy levels.
source: Mitofusin activation with MiM111 after axotomy restored mitochondrial motility and neuronal outgrowth to pre-axotomy levels.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing increased axon length in MiM111-treated neurons after axotomy.

claim: The link between experimentally activating mitofusins, the subsequent increase in mitochondrial transport, and enhanced neuronal growth/repair was consistent across multiple experimental models.
source: Thus, the link between experimentally activating mitofusins, the subsequent increase in mitochondrial transport, and enhanced neuronal growth/repair was consistent for mouse CMT2A sciatic nerve axons in vivo, cultured CMT2A DRG neuron outgrowth, and cultured CMT2A cortical nerve regrowth after distal axotomy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent findings across Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: This is the first report of any experimental intervention that fully reverses in vivo CMT2A phenotypes.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of any experimental intervention that fully reverses in vivo CMT2A phenotypes, demonstrating the feasibility of a clinically translatable disease-modifying therapeutic modality for this incurable condition.
evidence: This represents a claim about the novelty of the findings based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of a clinically translatable disease-modifying therapeutic modality for CMT2A.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of any experimental intervention that fully reverses in vivo CMT2A phenotypes, demonstrating the feasibility of a clinically translatable disease-modifying therapeutic modality for this incurable condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive preclinical data showing efficacy.

claim: Motor neurons directly reprogrammed from CMT2A patient fibroblasts have not previously been described.
source: Motor neurons directly reprogrammed from CMT2A patient fibroblasts have not previously been described, and provided a platform in which effects of therapeutic interventions could be assessed on different patients' mutations and individual genetic backgrounds using a disease-relevant cell type.
evidence: This represents a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Direct reprogramming more faithfully reproduced prototypical CMT2A mitochondrial phenotypes compared to iPS cell-derived CMT2A neurons.
source: Compared to iPS cell-derived CMT2A neurons (Rizzo et al., 2016; Saporta et al., 2015), direct reprogramming more faithfully reproduced prototypical CMT2A mitochondrial phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited studies and the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The CMT2A mouse model more faithfully recapitulates CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction compared to other CMT2A mice.
source: However, compared to other CMT2A mice, the current model more faithfully recapitulates CMT2A neuromuscular dysfunction that is the dominant cause of morbidity in the human condition (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the model characteristics (Figure 2) with clinical features described in the citations.

claim: The functional, histological, and ultrastructural features of axonal tissue in the CMT2A mice were similar to the human condition.
source: Moreover, the functional (neuroelectrophysiological), histological, and ultrastructural features of axonal tissue in the mice were similar to the human condition.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 showing similar features to those described in clinical CMT2A.

claim: Mitofusin activation reversed the signs of CMT2A in mice with severe, stable disease.
source: Perhaps the most remarkable finding here is that mitofusin activation reversed the signs of CMT2A in mice with severe, stable disease.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3 and 4 showing improvement in multiple disease parameters in 50-week-old mice with established disease.

claim: Every measured endpoint was improved after mitofusin activation in CMT2A mice.
source: Every measured endpoint was improved, including gross neuromuscular function (RotaRod), electrophysiological metrics of neuromuscular integrity (CMAP), read-outs for axon degeneration, and multiple histological and ultrastructural assays of mitochondrial pathology in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data throughout Figures 3 and 4 showing improvements in all measured parameters.

claim: In vivo and in vitro results pointed to enhanced CMT2A neuron repair and regrowth as a central reason for phenotype reversal.
source: In vivo and in vitro results pointed to enhanced CMT2A neuron repair and regrowth as a central reason for phenotype reversal.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing increased SCG10 staining (Figure 4a), increased axon diameter (Figure 4b), and enhanced neuron outgrowth (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: It is not possible to functionally dissociate mitofusin-mediated increases in mitochondrial fusion and motility.
source: Because it is not possible to functionally dissociate mitofusin-mediated increases in mitochondrial fusion and motility, it is unclear if one or the other of these responses preferentially underlies the neuroregenerative effects of mitofusin activation.
evidence: This represents a limitation of the experimental approach and current understanding of mitofusin function.

claim: Mitochondrial delivery to distal neurons likely has greatest importance in long peripheral nerves innervating hands, forearms, feet, and forelegs.
source: However, it seems reasonable to postulate that mitochondrial delivery to distal neurons has greatest importance in the long peripheral nerves innervating hands, forearms, feet, and forelegs, i.e. those areas most impacted in CMT2A (Fridman et al., 2015; Feely et al., 2011; Bombelli et al., 2014; Yaron and Schuldiner, 2016; Berciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the clinical pattern of CMT2A and the role of mitochondrial transport.

claim: There was a positive correlation between mitochondrial delivery to or occupancy of axonal termini and CMT2A neuron growth in vivo and in vitro.
source: In agreement with this notion, we observed a positive correlation between mitochondrial delivery to or occupancy of axonal termini and CMT2A neuron growth in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased mitochondrial occupancy at synapses (Figure 4d) and axonal termini (Figures 5f and 5—figure supplement 1c) correlating with improved neuron growth.

claim: Damaging MFN2 mutations are a straightforward cause of CMT2A.
source: As introduced above, damaging MFN2 mutations are a straightforward cause of CMT2A, but MFN2 multifunctionality complicates delineating the underlying cellular pathology (Filadi et al., 2018; Dorn, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MFN2 multifunctionality complicates delineating the underlying cellular pathology in CMT2A.
source: As introduced above, damaging MFN2 mutations are a straightforward cause of CMT2A, but MFN2 multifunctionality complicates delineating the underlying cellular pathology (Filadi et al., 2018; Dorn, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing the multiple functions of MFN2.

claim: The specific functional benefits accruing from mitofusin activation in CMT2A cannot unambiguously be defined.
source: For this reason, the specific functional benefits accruing from mitofusin activation in CMT2A cannot unambiguously be defined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the complexity of MFN2 function and the limitations of the current study.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and motility are impaired in CMT2A.
source: Mitochondrial fusion and motility are impaired in CMT2A (Chen and Chan, 2006) and allosteric mitofusin activation corrects both of these parameters (Franco et al., 2016; Rocha et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Allosteric mitofusin activation corrects impaired mitochondrial fusion and motility in CMT2A.
source: Mitochondrial fusion and motility are impaired in CMT2A (Chen and Chan, 2006) and allosteric mitofusin activation corrects both of these parameters (Franco et al., 2016; Rocha et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data throughout the manuscript showing improvements in these parameters.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction is a consequence of diminished fusion-mediated homeostatic repair.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction, measured here as loss of inner membrane polarization, is a consequence of diminished fusion-mediated homeostatic repair (Chen and Chan, 2006), and its improvement can therefore also be explained by enhanced fusogenicity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen and Chan, 2006 and represents established understanding of mitochondrial function.

claim: MFN2 has a role in mitophagic mitochondrial quality and quantity control.
source: MFN2 has a role in mitophagic mitochondrial quality and quantity control (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015), and allosteric mitofusin activation suppressed the increase in autophagy/mitophagy induced by CMT2A mutant MFN2 T105M in cultured cells (Rocha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015; and Rocha et al., 2018.

claim: Allosteric mitofusin activation suppressed the increase in autophagy/mitophagy induced by CMT2A mutant MFN2 T105M in cultured cells.
source: MFN2 has a role in mitophagic mitochondrial quality and quantity control (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015), and allosteric mitofusin activation suppressed the increase in autophagy/mitophagy induced by CMT2A mutant MFN2 T105M in cultured cells (Rocha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rocha et al., 2018.

claim: MFN2 can mediate physical interactions and calcium signaling between mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that may have a role in CMT2A.
source: Finally, MFN2 can mediate physical interactions and calcium signaling between mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that may also have a role in CMT2A (Larrea et al., 2019), but effects of mitofusin activation on mitochondria-reticular interactions have not been described.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Larrea et al., 2019.

claim: Effects of mitofusin activation on mitochondria-reticular interactions have not been described.
source: Finally, MFN2 can mediate physical interactions and calcium signaling between mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that may also have a role in CMT2A (Larrea et al., 2019), but effects of mitofusin activation on mitochondria-reticular interactions have not been described.
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Mitofusin activators are the first class of drugs to directly enhance mitochondrial fusion and transport.
source: Here, we studied two structurally distinct but functionally similar allosteric mitofusin activators, a new class of drug that is the first to directly enhance mitochondrial fusion and transport.
evidence: This represents a claim about the novelty of the drug class.

claim: A new generation of mitofusin activators have addressed pharmaceutical limitations of the initial chemical series.
source: Although the prototype compounds were found not to be 'druggable', a new generation of mitofusin activators have addressed pharmaceutical limitations of the initial chemical series (Dang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2020.

claim: Mitofusin activators have minimal effects in normal cells.
source: As described previously (Rocha et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2020), mitofusin activators have minimal effects in normal cells, likely because increasing the probability that mitofusins are in their open/ 'active' conformation is a subtle intervention that can be readily compensated for in the absence of a pre-existing imbalance between mitochondrial fusion and fission.
evidence: This is supported by citations and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Continuous long-term activation of mitochondrial fusion and transport might possibly be deleterious.
source: We considered that continuous long-term activation of mitochondrial fusion and transport might possibly be deleterious (El Fissi et al., 2018) (although it is worth noting that adverse effects of MFN1 and MFN2 overexpression in transgenic mice have not been reported).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on citation to El Fissi et al., 2018.

claim: Adverse effects of MFN1 and MFN2 overexpression in transgenic mice have not been reported.
source: We considered that continuous long-term activation of mitochondrial fusion and transport might possibly be deleterious (El Fissi et al., 2018) (although it is worth noting that adverse effects of MFN1 and MFN2 overexpression in transgenic mice have not been reported).
evidence: This represents current knowledge in the field.

claim: The problem underlying CMT2A is the cumulative effects of long-term mitochondrial stasis and dysfunction on mitochondrial fitness and neuromuscular integrity.
source: Moreover, we reasoned that the problem underlying CMT2A is the cumulative effects of long-term mitochondrial stasis and dysfunction on mitochondrial fitness and neuromuscular integrity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the progressive nature of the disease and the data presented.

claim: CMT2A progresses over many years in people and many weeks in mice.
source: This scenario can explain why CMT2A progresses over many years in people and many weeks in mice.
evidence: This is supported by clinical knowledge and data in Figure 2c showing progressive decline in mouse function.

claim: Human neuroregenerative capacity declines with age.
source: A mouse is not a man and human neuroregenerative capacity declines with age (Mattson and Magnus, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mattson and Magnus, 2006.

claim: Mitofusin activation may not fully reverse CMT2A phenotypes in older human patients with long-term stable disease.
source: For this reason we do not expect that mitofusin activation can fully reverse CMT2A phenotypes in older human patients with long-term stable disease.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the difference between mouse and human regenerative capacity.

claim: Pharmacological mitofusin activation could offer the first disease-altering therapy for younger CMT2A patients.
source: Nevertheless, the current results suggest that pharmacological mitofusin activation could offer the first disease-altering therapy for younger CMT2A patients.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the preclinical data presented.

claim: Mitofusin activation may have a therapeutic role in other neurodegenerative conditions where mitochondrial fusion or transport are defective.
source: An intriguing possibility is that mitofusin activation may also have a therapeutic role in some of the many other neurodegenerative conditions not directly caused by mitofusin defects wherein mitochondrial fusion or transport are defective (Dang et al., in preparation; Knott et al., 2008; Burté et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the mechanism of action and citations to other neurodegenerative conditions.

claim: Reprogramming efficiency was similar between CMT2A and control patient fibroblasts, with >90% neurons and >85% motor neurons.
source: Reprogramming efficiency was similar between CMT2A and control patient fibroblasts:>90% neurons (measured as β-III tubulin staining), and >85% motor neurons (measured as β-III tubulin, HB9/MNX1 co-staining) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Chimera C enhanced mitochondrial fusion in cells lacking either MFN1 or MFN2.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) enhanced mitochondrial fusion (i.e. it increased aspect ratio) and improved respiratory function (i.e. it reversed mitochondrial depolarization) in cells lacking either MFN1 or MFN2, but had no effects in cells lacking both mitofusin targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing increased aspect ratio in Mfn1 KO and Mfn2 KO MEFs but not in DKO MEFs.

claim: Chimera C improved respiratory function in cells lacking either MFN1 or MFN2.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) enhanced mitochondrial fusion (i.e. it increased aspect ratio) and improved respiratory function (i.e. it reversed mitochondrial depolarization) in cells lacking either MFN1 or MFN2, but had no effects in cells lacking both mitofusin targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing decreased depolarization in Mfn1 KO and Mfn2 KO MEFs but not in DKO MEFs.

claim: Chimera C had no effects in cells lacking both mitofusin targets.
source: Chimera C (100 nM, 48 hr) enhanced mitochondrial fusion (i.e. it increased aspect ratio) and improved respiratory function (i.e. it reversed mitochondrial depolarization) in cells lacking either MFN1 or MFN2, but had no effects in cells lacking both mitofusin targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing no change in aspect ratio or depolarization in DKO MEFs after Chimera C treatment.

claim: MFN2 T105M mouse tibialis myofiber atrophy mimicked clinical CMT2A.
source: Tibialis myofiber atrophy and loss of large axons without demyelination in the MFN2 T105M mouse (vide infra) also mimicked clinical CMT2A (Verhoeven et al., 2006; Muglia et al., 2001; Neves and Kok, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4c and citations to clinical studies.

claim: Loss of large axons without demyelination in the MFN2 T105M mouse mimicked clinical CMT2A.
source: Tibialis myofiber atrophy and loss of large axons without demyelination in the MFN2 T105M mouse (vide infra) also mimicked clinical CMT2A (Verhoeven et al., 2006; Muglia et al., 2001; Neves and Kok, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4b and citations to clinical studies.

claim: MiM111 plasma t1/2 is 2.3 hr after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg.
source: Based on a minimum effective MiM111 plasma concentration of 30 ng/ml (Dang et al., 2020) and a plasma t1/2 of 2.3 hr with Cmax of 24,000 ng/ml after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we estimated that daily IM dosing would reverse mitochondrial dysmotility in CMT2A mice for ~12 hr out of every 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MiM111 Cmax is 24,000 ng/ml after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg.
source: Based on a minimum effective MiM111 plasma concentration of 30 ng/ml (Dang et al., 2020) and a plasma t1/2 of 2.3 hr with Cmax of 24,000 ng/ml after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we estimated that daily IM dosing would reverse mitochondrial dysmotility in CMT2A mice for ~12 hr out of every 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The minimum effective MiM111 plasma concentration is 30 ng/ml.
source: Based on a minimum effective MiM111 plasma concentration of 30 ng/ml (Dang et al., 2020) and a plasma t1/2 of 2.3 hr with Cmax of 24,000 ng/ml after intramuscular administration of 30 mg/kg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we estimated that daily IM dosing would reverse mitochondrial dysmotility in CMT2A mice for ~12 hr out of every 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2020.

claim: The aspect ratio of mitochondria in the distal linear axons of normal and CMT2A neurons was unaffected by axotomy.
source: The aspect ratio of mitochondria in the distal linear axons of normal and CMT2A neurons was unaffected either by axotomy or by MiM111 (Figure 6d, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing no change in aspect ratio after axotomy.

claim: The aspect ratio of mitochondria in the distal linear axons of normal and CMT2A neurons was unaffected by MiM111.
source: The aspect ratio of mitochondria in the distal linear axons of normal and CMT2A neurons was unaffected either by axotomy or by MiM111 (Figure 6d, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing no change in aspect ratio with MiM111 treatment in the axotomy model.
